Part IV - Service¶

The core (Parts I-III) and the user interface are separate processes. This part defines what connects them: a wire protocol (Section 1), the session that owns a reconstruction (Section 2), the assembly of a model from a data folder or a run and the jobs that advance it (Section 3), the server (Section 4), the client (Section 5) and the command line (Section 6). Only protocol and client are needed on the interface side; they import neither PyTorch nor the physics.

Part IV, Section 1: the wire protocol between the core and a client.

Theory¶

The reconstruction core and the user interface are two processes. They share no memory and no objects; everything that crosses the boundary is one message, which consists of

  • a JSON header (a dictionary), and

  • any number of binary arrays whose dtype and shape are listed in the header (header["arrays"]), each sent as one raw buffer.

On the wire a message is a list of frames, [header, buffer_1, ..., buffer_n], so that images are never converted to text. The transport (ZeroMQ DEALER/ROUTER, see temsim.service.server) adds an identity frame in front.

Three kinds of messages exist.

command (client -> core)

{"kind": "command", "id": k, "name": ..., "args": {...}}. Exactly one reply with the same id follows. Commands are executed by the single owner of the model between two optimisation steps (Section 2); the order in which a client sends them is the order in which they take effect.

reply (core -> client)

{"kind": "reply", "id": k, "ok": true, "result": {...}} or, on failure, {"ok": false, "error": "...", "trace": "..."}. A failing command never changes the model.

event (core -> every client that has said hello)

{"kind": "event", "name": ..., "data": {...}}. Events are status (idle / running / paused), light (step and loss, cheap, every step), frame (images and atoms, throttled), log (text) and error.

Data classes of temsim.data.schema travel as the JSON of temsim.data.codec; the bulk arrays of the training settings (masks, group targets) travel as binary arrays named mask.<group> and target.<group>.

The module imports numpy and the data layer only. A client therefore needs neither PyTorch nor the physics.

Note

The server binds to 127.0.0.1 by default and accepts commands from anyone who can reach the port; a remote core is reached through an SSH tunnel, never by opening the port.

Part IV, Section 2: the session, the one owner of a reconstruction.

Theory¶

A reconstruction is a sequence of states; the optimiser (Part II, Section 5) and the seeding (Part II, Section 6) move from one state to the next. Everything that a person does in the meantime – switching a parameter, changing a weight, deleting weak atoms, inserting candidate sites – is a change of state between two steps. To make this well defined the model has exactly one owner, the Session, and every access goes through it. The session is not thread safe by design: the server (Section 4) calls it from one thread only and interleaves the commands of the clients with the steps of the running job.

The session answers three kinds of requests.

Queries change nothing: Session.info(), Session.frame() (images, atoms, optional extras), Session.minima().

Settings change the objective or the switches, never the parameters: set_param(), set_loss(), … Because the model reads its settings at every step (Part II, Section 4) they act on the next step without rebuilding anything. The optimiser keeps the Adam moments of all tensors that stay trainable (Part II, Section 5).

Edits change the parameters or the atom list (edit(), insert_minima()). After an edit the seeder re-reads the state (resync()) because its running sums (Part II, Eq. 6.4) are only valid for the state they were computed from.

The frame is the picture of the state that a client draws. It contains

  • the simulated image \(s\), the measured image \(t\) and the difference \(\delta = x - y\) of the standardised images (Part II, Eq. 2.2),

  • the mask of the active group,

  • for every layer the effective positions \(\mathbf r^{\rm eff}\) (Part I, Eq. 1.2), the occupancies \(o\) and the intensities \(I\),

and, on request, the optics (phase of the transfer function and the aperture ring in TEM, the probe in STEM), the strain maps of the active group, the projected potentials, and the gradient \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\,\Delta\mathbf r\) of the loss with respect to the free position shifts. Positions are in pixels (row, column) throughout.

Part IV, Section 3: from a data folder (or a run) to a model.

Theory¶

Parts I-III describe the pieces; the user wants to start from a folder with a measurement. Three routes lead to a reconstruction problem.

Lattice route (the ImageJ plug-in). The folder says which lattices exist, which layer of which lattice fills which experiment layer, and what is trained. Each lattice has to cover the image after the largest allowed rigid motion of the groups that use it (Part III, Eq. 3.1: canvas_size_px), so its reach is

\[\Delta_{\max}(\text{lattice}) = \max_{g \in \text{groups using it}}\ \Delta_g, \qquad \vartheta_{\max}(\text{lattice}) = \max_{g}\ \vartheta_g .\]

The height of an experiment layer is its z_nm if the folder gives one; the data model cannot distinguish “not given” from 0, therefore the rule is: if all layers of a lattice are at z_nm == 0 while the lattice has layers at different heights, the heights of the lattice (plus its z_offset_nm) are used.

Seeding route (no lattice). The model starts with one empty layer of the first group; the seeding of Part II, Section 6 fills it. Only the microscope is trained meanwhile (aberrations, normalisation), and the loss counts the image without a border of border_px pixels where the multislice and the probe are cut off (Part I, Section 9). When the seeded layer is saved for further training the settings are changed to those of a refinement: positions and intensities are released, a repulsion keeps neighbours apart, all other priors are off, and only defocus and spherical aberration are trained.

Run route. A run directory (any layout, Part III, Section 3) already contains specification, settings and state; the target is the one stored with it or the target of the folder that contains it.

Implementation¶

This module is plain data wrangling (numpy and the lattice generator of Part I; the seeding start imports one helper of Part II lazily). Its result is an Assembly; the Session turns it into a model.

Part IV, Section 3: jobs and their pacing.

Theory¶

Optimisation and seeding are long; a user wants to watch and to intervene. Both are therefore cut into units of work that are small compared with the time a person needs to notice a delay:

  • a training job advances one optimiser step (Part II, Eq. 5.1) per unit,

  • a seeding job advances a chunk of trials (Part II, Section 6) per unit, followed by a tuning phase of a few optimiser steps every tune_every trials.

Between two units the server (Section 4) handles all waiting commands. A command therefore never sees a half-finished step, and a pause is simply “do not advance”.

Drawing a frame costs a full simulation and is much slower than a step. The Clock decides when the next frame is due: after a frame that took \(c\) seconds the next one is not before \(\max(T_{\rm min},\,\kappa c)\) seconds, so that at most \(1/(1+\kappa)\) of the time goes into drawing (kappa = 3 keeps it below 25 %). The cheap light message (step, loss) is sent every unit.

Implementation¶

Part IV, Section 4: the server.

Theory¶

The server is a single loop that alternates between listening and working:

repeat
    handle every waiting command           (at most ``MAX_BATCH`` per round)
    if a job is running:  advance it by one unit; publish light / frame / autosave
    else:                 wait for the next command

so that, as stated in Section 2, the model is only ever touched by this one thread and commands take effect between two units of work. Transport is a ZeroMQ ROUTER socket: every client is a DEALER whose identity the router sees, which makes replies (to one client) and events (to every client that has said hello) the same kind of send.

Failure is contained. A command that raises is answered with ok = false and a traceback; a job that raises is ended and reported as an error event; neither stops the server. Only shutdown does.

Implementation¶

Part IV, Section 5: the client.

Theory¶

A client is anything that speaks the protocol of Section 1: the Qt interface, a script, a test. It needs neither PyTorch nor the physics; this module imports numpy, pyzmq and the data layer.

A DEALER socket may be used by one thread only. The client therefore owns a transport thread that holds the socket; other threads hand it outgoing messages through an in-process queue (inproc PUSH/PULL pair, which also wakes the thread) and wait for the reply with the matching id. Incoming events are delivered to on_event(name, data, arrays) in the transport thread; a graphical client must forward them to its own thread (for Qt: emit a signal).

Calls are synchronous (Client.call()) and time out; a timed-out call does not cancel the command, which may still run on the core.

Part IV, Section 6: the command line.

python -m temsim.service serve starts a core; python -m temsim.service ping asks a running core for its description. The core binds to 127.0.0.1 unless told otherwise (see the note in temsim.service.protocol).
